intro: Somewhere this year a word is going to stop you. It will be twelve letters long, sitting in the middle of a science test or a history article, and you will have never seen it before. This unit gives you two ways past it. The first is to take the word apart. English is stuffed with parts borrowed from Greek and Latin, and about twenty of them, stems like bio, graph, port and dict, show up in thousands of words. Learn the parts and you can build meanings you never memorized.

The second way is to read what a word carries. Thin, slender and scrawny mean the same thing in a dictionary, but nobody wants to be called scrawny. Words have feelings riding on their backs, and writers choose them on purpose. You will learn to hear the difference, to name a writer's tone, and to use a thesaurus without sounding like you swallowed one.

Then you will study the sentences that are not literally true and are true anyway: the classroom that was a zoo, the fog on cat feet, the hope with feathers. Similes, metaphors, personification, hyperbole, allusions and idioms run through poems, songs, ads and ordinary talk. By the end you will be able to take them apart, say what they mean, and write your own with words that are exact.
bigQuestion: How do word parts, word feelings and figures of speech let a reader unlock words and a writer choose them?

timeline.t: Greek thinkers use words like logos and bios that will become English stems two thousand years later.
Latin is spoken across the Roman Empire; portare, dicere and credere are everyday verbs.
The Normans conquer England, and French, a child of Latin, brings thousands of Latin words into English.
Shakespeare writes All the world's a stage, an extended metaphor still quoted today.
Robert Burns compares his love to a red, red rose in a simile English speakers still know.
Samuel Morse sends a message by telegraph, a machine named from Greek parts meaning far and write.
Emily Dickinson writes that hope is the thing with feathers, a metaphor that never names its bird.
Dickinson's hope poem is published, four years after her death, and readers meet the feathered thing.
Carl Sandburg's Chicago Poems gives the city fog little cat feet.
Scientists still build new words from Greek and Latin stems, and ads still sell with metaphors.

a word part added to the front of a stem that changes its meaning
a word part added to the end of a stem that often changes the word's job
a group of words that share a stem and part of their meaning, such as photograph and photosynthesis
the plain dictionary meaning of a word
the feeling or association a word carries beyond its dictionary meaning
the writer's attitude toward the subject, shown through word choice
a comparison of two unlike things using like or as
a comparison that says one thing is another, without like or as
giving human actions, feelings or qualities to something that is not human
deliberate exaggeration used for effect, not meant to be taken literally
a brief reference to a well-known story, person, place or event

test.q: In the word prediction, which part is the stem?
test.why: Dict, from a Latin word meaning say, carries the core meaning. Pre is a prefix and ion is a suffix.
Bio is the Greek stem for life, as in biology and biography.

test.q: Using its parts, what does telescope let you do?
test.why: Tele means far and scope comes from a Greek word for looking.

test.q: Which word means a bad function or a machine working badly?
test.why: Mal means bad, so a malfunction is when something works badly.

test.q: Why did so many Latin words enter English after 1066?
choices: Roman soldiers settled in England that year
The Normans brought French, which grew out of Latin
test.why: After the Norman conquest, French became the language of law and the court, carrying Latin-based words with it.

test.q: What should you do after building a rough meaning from a word's parts?
choices: Look up the word in Greek
Check the meaning against the sentence
Skip the word if the parts are Latin
test.why: Some words have drifted from their roots, like manufacture, so the sentence must confirm the built meaning.

test.q: Which word belongs to the same word family as geology?
test.why: Geology and geography share the Greek stem geo, meaning earth.

test.q: Which word has a negative connotation for a low price?
test.why: Cheap has come to suggest badly made. The others stay neutral or polite.

choices: The dictionary meaning of a word
The feeling or association a word carries
The Greek origin of a word
The number of syllables in a word
test.why: Connotation is the feeling that rides along with a word, such as the sneer in scrawny.

choices: The test was like a mountain
The test glared at me from the desk
test.why: It states that one thing is another without like or as. The first is a simile, the second literal, the fourth personification.

choices: The soup was as hot as fresh coffee
The soup was hotter than the surface of the sun
test.why: Hotter than the sun is a deliberate exaggeration meant to show a feeling, not a fact.

test.q: In Sandburg's poem, the fog comes on little cat feet. Which figure of speech is this?
choices: Personification, giving the fog an animal's body and behavior
test.why: The fog is given a cat's feet and way of sitting and watching, a living creature's traits.

test.q: Calling a hidden danger a Trojan horse is which figure of speech?
test.why: It refers to the Greek story of the wooden horse that hid soldiers, so it is an allusion.

test.q: Which is true of an idiom like piece of cake?
choices: Its meaning can be built from its words
Its meaning must be learned as a whole phrase
It belongs in formal science reports
test.why: An idiom's meaning is not the sum of its words; piece of cake means easy and has nothing to do with dessert.

test.q: Which revision makes a sentence more precise?
choices: The bird flew becomes The bird went
The bird flew becomes The bird really flew
The bird flew becomes The animal moved
The bird flew becomes The hawk circled
test.why: Hawk and circled are specific, so the reader sees exactly what happened.

write.prompt: Make a claim: is a thesaurus a helpful tool or a dangerous one for a middle school writer? Support your claim with evidence from this unit about connotation, precise language and word parts, and explain your reasoning.
tips: State your claim in one clear sentence at the start: helpful, dangerous, or helpful only when used a certain way.
Use evidence from the unit: the canine was jubilant example, the difference between denotation and connotation, or how stems reveal a word's exact meaning.
Explain your reasoning: say why each piece of evidence supports your claim, not just that it does.
Address the other side in a sentence or two, then explain why your claim still stands.
End by telling a younger writer exactly what to do the next time they open a thesaurus.

title: Words: Stems and Meaning

chapters.title: Greek and Latin Stems
chapters.bigQuestion: How can twenty old word parts unlock thousands of words you have never seen?

story.title: The Test Word She Had Never Studied
story.kicker: A seventh grader meets a word on a biology test that was never on the study guide, and a stem from English class takes it apart.
paragraphs: Marisol stared at question fourteen on the life science test. It asked her to list two abiotic factors in a pond. She had studied the food web. She had studied producers and consumers. She had never seen the word abiotic in her life. Her pencil stopped. Around her the room was quiet except for the click of the wall clock and someone's chair squeaking.

She almost skipped it. Then she looked at the word again, slowly, the way her English teacher had made the class look at words all fall. Bio. She knew bio. Biology was the study of life. A biography was the story of a life. So bio meant life. That left a small a at the front and a tic at the end. The ending did not worry her. Lots of describing words ended in ic: basic, magnetic, athletic.

The a at the front was the puzzle. Then she remembered a word from math class: asymmetrical, a shape that was not symmetrical. The a had flipped the word to its opposite. If abiotic worked the same way, it meant not living. Abiotic factors in a pond would be the parts that were never alive. Sunlight. Water. Temperature. Rocks and mud on the bottom.

She wrote down sunlight and water temperature and moved on. When the tests came back, question fourteen had a check mark next to it. Her teacher had written one word in the margin: Good. Marisol had not memorized abiotic. She had built its meaning from parts, the way you can read a number you have never seen because you know the digits.

That is what this chapter is about. English borrowed thousands of word parts from Greek and Latin. Scientists, doctors, lawyers and historians still use them to build new words. Learn twenty of these parts well and you carry a key that opens words in every class you take. Marisol's key was three letters long.
story.think: Think of a long word from science or social studies that stopped you this year. Can you see any smaller part inside it that you already know?

lessons.title: Stems, Prefixes and Suffixes
lessons.mainIdea: Many long English words are built from a stem that carries the core meaning, plus a prefix in front or a suffix behind.
reading: Look at the word transportation. It looks long, but it is built from three pieces. In the middle sits port, which comes from a Latin word meaning carry. In front is trans, meaning across. At the end is ation, which turns an action into a thing. Put the pieces together: the act of carrying something across. A bus, a train and a bike lane are all transportation.

The piece in the middle is the *stem*. Some teachers call it the root. A stem carries the main meaning of the word, but most stems from Greek and Latin cannot stand alone. Port is not an English word by itself in this sense; you do not port your books to school. It needs company. A *prefix* attaches to the front of a stem and changes its meaning. A *suffix* attaches to the end and often changes the word's job, turning a verb into a noun or an adjective.

Try it with the stem dict, from a Latin word meaning say. Add the prefix pre, meaning before, and you get predict: to say before it happens. Add the suffix ion and you get prediction, the thing you said. Swap in the prefix contra, meaning against, and you get contradict: to say the opposite of what someone else said. Same stem, three different words, and you can read all three.

Here is the habit to build. When a long word stops you, do not guess from the first letter. Find the stem in the middle first. Ask what it means. Then look at the front and the back for a prefix and a suffix. Say the parts out loud. Most of the time the meaning will fall into place, just as it did for Marisol on her biology test.

words.d: the part of a word that carries its core meaning; Greek and Latin stems usually cannot stand alone
a word part added to the front of a stem that changes the meaning, such as pre in predict
a word part added to the end of a stem that often changes the word's job, such as ion in prediction

look.title: Three Pieces
look.text: A student writes the word transportation on the board and draws two lines through it: trans | port | ation. Under each piece she writes one word: across, carry, the act of. Then she erases trans and writes ex. The class reads the new word: exportation, the act of carrying goods out of a country.
look.prompt: If you replaced ex with im, meaning in, what word would you get, and what would it mean?

check.q: Which part of the word transportation carries its core meaning?
check.why: Port is the stem, from a Latin word meaning carry. Trans is a prefix and ation is a suffix.

check.q: What does the prefix contra do to the stem dict in contradict?
choices: It makes the word a noun
It means against, so contradict means to say the opposite
It removes the meaning of dict
check.why: Contra means against. To contradict is to say something against what another person said.

check.q: What is the best first step when a long word stops you?
choices: Skip the word and keep reading
Find the stem in the middle and ask what it means
check.why: The lesson says to find the stem first, since it carries the core meaning, then check for a prefix and suffix.

lessons.title: Two Old Languages in English
lessons.mainIdea: English borrowed stems from Latin and from Greek, and knowing which language a stem comes from helps you spot where it shows up.
reading: English is a mix. Its everyday words, like house, bread, sun and run, mostly come from old Germanic roots. But when the Normans conquered England in 1066, French became the language of the court and the law for centuries. French grew out of Latin, so thousands of Latin words poured into English: justice, nation, port, credit. Later, scholars borrowed straight from Latin books.

Greek came in a different door. When scientists in the 1600s, 1700s and 1800s needed names for new things, they often built them from Greek parts. Telephone, photograph, biology, microscope and thermometer were all made this way, out of pieces that Greek speakers had used two thousand years earlier. That is why so many science and medical words feel Greek. They are.

You can often tell which family a stem belongs to. Latin stems tend to show up in law, government and everyday formal words: dict, port, cred, ject, rupt, spec, bene, mal. Greek stems crowd into science and technology: bio, geo, graph, log, chron, phon, tele, micro, poly, hydro, auto, anti. The two families also mix freely. Television is half Greek, tele, and half Latin, vision. Nobody stopped to check.

Why does the family matter to you? Because it tells you where to expect a stem. If you meet hydro in a chemistry text, you can guess it means water, since hydro is Greek and Greek stems fill science. If you meet a Latin stem like cred in a news story about banks, you can guess it has to do with believing or trusting. The family is a clue about the neighborhood the word lives in.

words.d: the language of ancient Rome; many English words for law, government and formal life come from it
the language of ancient Greece; many English science and technology words are built from Greek parts
the family of languages that gave English its oldest, plainest words, such as house and bread
