check.q: Why do so many science words in English come from Greek parts?
choices: Scientists in past centuries built new names out of Greek pieces
Greek was the language of the English court after 1066
Greek words are shorter than English words
All English words come from Greek
check.why: When scientists needed names for new discoveries, they often assembled them from Greek stems, such as telephone and biology.

check.q: How did most Latin words first enter English?
choices: Through French after the Norman conquest of 1066
check.why: French, which grew out of Latin, became the language of law and the court after 1066, and thousands of Latin-based words came with it.

check.q: The word television mixes two families. Which is true?
choices: Tele is Greek and vision is Latin
Tele is Latin and vision is Greek
check.why: Tele, meaning far, is Greek. Vision, from a Latin word for seeing, is Latin. English mixes them without trouble.

sections.title: Stems for Life, Earth and Writing

lessons.title: bio, geo and graph
lessons.mainIdea: Bio means life, geo means earth and graph means write or draw; together they build dozens of words in science and beyond.
reading: Start with *bio*, a Greek stem meaning life. Biology is the study of life. A biography is the written story of a person's life. An autobiography is a life story you write yourself. Antibiotics are medicines that work against tiny living things that make you sick. A biome is a large region of living things, like a desert or a forest. Every time you see bio, look for life.

Next is *geo*, Greek for earth. Geology is the study of the earth, its rocks and its layers. Geography is writing or drawing about the earth, which is why maps belong to it. A geode is a rock with crystals inside. In math, geometry began as the measuring of earth, the tool ancient people used to lay out fields and mark borders after floods.

The third stem is *graph*, from a Greek word meaning write or draw. A photograph is drawn by light. An autograph is a name written by the person who owns it. A paragraph is a group of written lines. A graph in math is a drawing of numbers. Notice how graph appears in both geography and photograph. That is a word family: different words that share a stem and share part of their meaning.

Here is a word you may meet in an Illinois science class: biogeography. It looks like a mouthful. Take it apart. Bio, life. Geo, earth. Graph, writing. Biogeography is the study of where living things live on the earth, and why. If you can build the meaning, you can read the whole page.

words.d: a Greek stem meaning life, as in biology and biography
a Greek stem meaning earth, as in geology and geography
a Greek stem meaning write or draw, as in photograph and paragraph

look.title: One Stem, Many Rooms
look.text: Picture a school hallway. In the science room a poster says Biology. In the library a shelf is labeled Biographies. In the nurse's office a bottle says Antibiotic. In the social studies room a map is titled Biomes of North America. Four rooms, four different words, one stem walking through all of them.
look.prompt: Choose one of the four words and explain how the stem bio and the other parts add up to its meaning.

check.q: What does an autobiography contain?
choices: A story of the writer's own life
check.why: Auto means self, bio means life and graph means write, so an autobiography is a life story written by the person who lived it.

check.q: Geometry began as which kind of activity?
choices: Measuring the earth to lay out fields
check.why: Geo means earth and metry means measuring. Ancient people used geometry to mark fields and borders.

check.q: What is a word family?
choices: Words that share a stem and part of their meaning
Words that all start with the same letter
Words that mean the opposite of each other
check.why: Geography, photograph and paragraph all share the stem graph, so they form a word family.

lessons.title: log, chron and phon
lessons.mainIdea: Log means word or study, chron means time and phon means sound; they name subjects, clocks and everything that has to do with sound.
reading: The stem *log* comes from the Greek word logos, which meant word, reason or study. That is why so many school subjects end in ology: biology, geology, psychology, technology. The ending means the study of. A dialogue is words spoken between two people. A logo is a picture that stands in for a company's name. A logical argument is one that follows reason step by step.

*Chron* means time. A chronological list is in time order, first to last. A chronic illness is one that lasts a long time. A chronicle is a record of events in the order they happened. Synchronized swimmers move at the same time. If you see chron in a history book, think about time, because that is what the word is measuring.

*Phon* means sound. A telephone carries sound far away. A microphone makes a small sound big. A symphony is sounds put together. Phonics, which you may remember from early grades, is the study of the sounds letters make. A homophone is a word that sounds the same as another word, like their and there.

Watch how the stems combine. Chronology is chron plus logy, the study of time order. Phonology is the study of sounds in language. Your history teacher and your science teacher may never mention Greek, but they hand you Greek words every week. Now you can hand the meanings back.

words.d: a Greek stem meaning word, reason or study; ology means the study of
a Greek stem meaning time, as in chronological and chronic
a Greek stem meaning sound, as in telephone and phonics

look.title: Parts in a Word
look.prompt: Which word has three parts, and what does each part mean? Which stem from this lesson appears in more than one word on the list?

check.q: A chronological list of events is arranged how?
choices: By how important each event was
In time order, first to last
By how many people were involved
check.why: Chron means time, so a chronological list follows the order in which things happened.

check.q: Which word means a sound that is made bigger?
check.why: Micro means small and phon means sound: a microphone takes a small sound and makes it loud.

check.q: Psychology ends in ology. What does that ending tell you?
choices: The word names the study of something
The word is a kind of picture
check.why: Ology comes from logos and means the study of. Psychology is the study of the mind.

lessons.title: spec and port
lessons.mainIdea: Spec means look and port means carry; both are Latin stems that appear in hundreds of everyday words.
reading: The Latin stem *spec* means look or see. You already know inspect, to look closely into something. A spectator looks at a game. Spectacles are glasses you look through. A spectacular sunset is one worth looking at. To respect someone is, in the oldest sense, to look back at them with care. When you suspect something, you look at it with doubt. The stem sometimes changes its spelling to spect or spic, as in conspicuous, easy to see.

The Latin stem *port* means carry. A porter carries luggage. To transport is to carry across. To import is to carry goods into a country, and to export is to carry them out. A portable speaker is one you can carry. Even a report carries information back to someone. The seaport where ships carry goods in and out shares the same stem.

Chicago has a lot of port words. It sits on Lake Michigan and grew rich because goods were carried in and out by water and rail. O'Hare is an airport. Trucks on the highways are part of transportation. The city itself was a port long before it had skyscrapers.

Try two hard words. Introspection: intro means inside, spec means look, tion makes it a thing. Introspection is looking inside yourself at your own thoughts. Deportation: de means away, port means carry, ation makes it a thing. Deportation is being carried away out of a country. Two words you might never have studied, and you can read both.

words.d: a Latin stem meaning look or see, as in inspect and spectator; sometimes spelled spect
a Latin stem meaning carry, as in transport and portable
to carry goods into a country; the opposite of export

look.title: A Model Paragraph
look.text: The inspector walked the dock at the port and looked at every crate. A spectator would have seen only boxes. She saw an import that had no papers, a portable scale that was broken, and a report she would have to write before dinner.
look.prompt: Find every word in the paragraph built on spec or port. For each one, say what the stem contributes to its meaning.

check.q: What does the stem spec mean in the word spectator?
check.why: A spectator is someone who looks at an event. Spec comes from a Latin word meaning look or see.

check.q: Based on the stems, what is introspection?
choices: Looking inside yourself at your own thoughts
check.why: Intro means inside and spec means look. Introspection is examining your own thoughts.

check.q: Which word means to carry goods out of a country?
check.why: Ex means out and port means carry, so to export is to carry goods out of a country.

sections.title: Stems for Action, Judgment and Distance

lessons.title: rupt, ject and dict
lessons.mainIdea: Rupt means break, ject means throw and dict means say; each is a Latin stem for a strong action.
reading: The stem *rupt* means break. A pipe ruptures when it breaks open. An interruption breaks into a conversation. A volcano erupts when it breaks out. A corrupt official is one whose honesty has been broken. A bankrupt business is one whose money has run out, from an old Italian custom of breaking a money changer's bench when he failed. All of these words share the picture of something breaking.

The stem *ject* means throw. To reject a plan is to throw it back. To eject a disc is to throw it out. To inject medicine is to throw it in, with a needle. A projectile is something thrown forward. Even the word object, in its oldest sense, was a thing thrown in your way. When you see ject, picture an arm throwing.

The stem *dict* means say. A dictionary is a book of things said, or words. To dictate is to say words aloud for someone to write down. A verdict is a truth said by a jury at the end of a trial. A dictator is a ruler whose word is law. A prediction says what will happen before it does.

Notice how the same prefixes keep coming back. Inter, meaning between, gives you interrupt and interject. Pre, meaning before, gives you predict and prevent. E or ex, meaning out, gives you erupt, eject and exit. Once you know a dozen prefixes and a dozen stems, you can mix and match them into far more words than you memorized.

words.d: a Latin stem meaning break, as in erupt and interrupt
a Latin stem meaning throw, as in reject and inject
a Latin stem meaning say, as in dictionary and verdict
the decision a jury says at the end of a trial; literally, a truth said

look.title: The Courtroom Word
look.text: A jury files back into a courtroom. The judge asks the foreperson to read the verdict. Vere is Latin for truly, and dict means say. For a moment the word is not a courtroom term at all. It is just two Latin pieces: truly said. Then the foreperson says guilty or not guilty, and the word is a verdict again.
look.prompt: Predict is pre plus dict. Using the same method, what is a contradiction, and why is that a good name for it?

check.q: What picture do all the rupt words share?
check.why: Rupt means break. Erupt, interrupt, rupture and corrupt all involve breaking in some way.

check.q: Which word means to throw something back?
check.why: Re means back and ject means throw, so to reject is to throw back.

check.q: A dictator is a ruler whose word is law. Which stem explains the name?
check.why: Dict means say. A dictator's sayings are commands that everyone must obey.

lessons.title: cred, bene and mal
lessons.mainIdea: Cred means believe, bene means good or well, and mal means bad; these stems tell you whether a word is about trust, help or harm.
reading: The Latin stem *cred* means believe. A credible story is one you can believe. An incredible story is one you cannot believe, though today people also use it to mean amazing. Your credit at a store is the trust that you will pay later. A creed is a statement of beliefs. When a witness is discredited, people stop believing her. The stem asks one question: can this be trusted?

The stem *bene* means good or well. A benefit is a good result. A benefactor is someone who does good for others, often by giving money. A benediction is a good saying, a blessing. If a doctor says a growth is benign, that is the good news: it is harmless. Bene is the stem you want to hear.

The stem *mal* means bad. Malnutrition is bad nourishment, not enough food. A malfunction is when a machine works badly. Malice is the wish to do harm. Malware is software written to do bad things to your computer. A malignant growth is the dangerous kind. Bene and mal are opposites, and doctors, lawyers and computer technicians use both every day.

Try a word from the news: malpractice. Mal means bad, practice means the work a professional does. Malpractice is when a doctor or lawyer does the job badly enough to cause harm. Now try benevolent. Bene means good, and vol comes from a Latin word for wishing. A benevolent person wishes others well. You just read two college-level words.

words.d: a Latin stem meaning believe, as in credible and credit
a Latin stem meaning good or well, as in benefit and benign
a Latin stem meaning bad, as in malfunction and malware

look.title: The Doctor's Two Words
look.text: A patient sits in a clinic waiting to hear one of two words about a test result. If the doctor says benign, the growth is harmless. If the doctor says malignant, it is dangerous and needs treatment. The patient has never studied Latin, but she leans forward when she hears the first syllable.
look.prompt: Why is it useful for a patient to know the stems bene and mal before hearing a diagnosis? What other mal words might a nurse use?

check.q: What does the stem cred ask about a word?
choices: Whether something can be believed or trusted
check.why: Cred means believe. Credible, credit and creed all involve believing or trusting.

check.q: A benefactor is best described as which of these?
choices: A person who believes a story
A person who does good for others
A saying at the end of a trial
check.why: Bene means good, and a benefactor is someone who does good for others, often with money.

check.q: Based on the stems, what is malnutrition?
check.why: Mal means bad. Malnutrition is bad nourishment, usually from not getting enough food or the right food.

lessons.title: anti, auto and tele
lessons.mainIdea: Anti means against, auto means self and tele means far; these three Greek prefixes appear on the front of many modern words.
reading: Some stems almost always sit at the front of a word, so people call them prefixes. *Anti* means against. An antibiotic works against living germs. Antifreeze works against freezing. An antonym is a word against another word, its opposite. The Antarctic is the region opposite the Arctic. Do not confuse anti with ante, which means before, as in anteroom, the room before the main room.

*Auto* means self. An automobile moves by itself, without a horse. An autograph is written by the person's own self. An autobiography is a life story written by the self. Automatic doors open by themselves. In social studies, autonomy is self-rule, the right of a people to govern themselves.

*Tele* means far or distant. A telephone carries sound far. A telescope lets you look far. A television carries pictures far. Telecommuting is working far from the office. When the word telegraph was invented in the 1800s, it meant exactly what its pieces said: writing sent far, over a wire.

These three prefixes love to join other stems from this chapter. Anti plus bio plus tic gives antibiotic. Auto plus graph gives autograph. Tele plus phon gives telephone. Tele plus scope, from a Greek word for looking, gives telescope. When you meet a new word starting with anti, auto or tele, cut the prefix off first and see what stem is left.

words.d: a Greek prefix meaning against or opposite, as in antibiotic and antonym
a Greek prefix meaning self, as in automatic and autobiography
a Greek prefix meaning far or distant, as in telephone and telescope
self-rule; the right of a group of people to govern themselves

look.title: Two Wires and a Word
look.text: In 1844 the inventor Samuel Morse sent a message from Washington to Baltimore over a telegraph wire. The device's name had been built from Greek parts: tele, far, and graph, write. The message was writing that traveled far in an instant.
look.cite: Samuel Morse's first long-distance telegraph message, 1844 (described, not quoted)
look.prompt: Morse used a Greek name for a brand-new machine. Why might inventors reach for old Greek parts instead of inventing a wholly new word?

check.q: Which word means the opposite of another word?
check.why: Ant comes from anti, meaning against, and onym means name or word. An antonym is a word set against another.

check.q: In social studies, autonomy means what?
choices: Self-rule by a group of people
check.why: Auto means self, so autonomy is the right of a people to govern themselves.

check.q: What did the pieces of the word telegraph mean when it was invented?
check.why: Tele means far and graph means write. A telegraph sent written messages over long distances.

lessons.title: micro, poly and hydro
lessons.mainIdea: Micro means small, poly means many and hydro means water; they fill science words in biology, chemistry, geography and math.
reading: The Greek stem *micro* means small. A microscope lets you look at small things. A microphone makes small sounds loud. A microwave oven uses short waves. Microbes are tiny living things. In economics, microeconomics studies small units like one family or one store. Its opposite is macro, meaning large.

The stem *poly* means many. A polygon is a shape with many angles and sides. Polyester is a fabric made from many linked chemical units. A polyglot is a person who speaks many languages. Polytheism is belief in many gods, and monotheism, with mono meaning one, is belief in one. In math class you may meet polynomials, expressions with many terms.

The stem *hydro* means water. Hydrogen is the element that, when burned, makes water. A hydrant gives water to firefighters. Hydroelectric power comes from moving water, like the dams on the Mississippi River. A hydroplane skims across water. To hydrate your body is to give it water. Dehydration, with de meaning away, is losing water.

Look at a word from a biology textbook: microorganism. Micro, small. Organism, a living thing. A microorganism is a living thing too small to see. Now a word from chemistry: hydrophobic. Hydro, water. Phobic, fearing or avoiding. A hydrophobic surface pushes water away, like a waxed car hood. Each time, the parts told you the meaning before the teacher did.

words.d: a Greek stem meaning small, as in microscope and microbe
a Greek stem meaning many, as in polygon and polyglot
a Greek stem meaning water, as in hydrogen and hydrate

look.title: Sides in Poly Shapes
look.prompt: Every shape here is a polygon, a many-angled shape. Each name uses a Greek number word before gon. What number does each prefix stand for, and which one do you already know from a month or a sea creature?

check.q: What does a microscope let you do?
check.why: Micro means small and scope means look. A microscope lets you look at very small objects.

check.q: What is the difference between polytheism and monotheism?
choices: Poly means water and mono means small
Poly means many gods and mono means one god
Poly means one god and mono means many
check.why: Poly means many and mono means one, so polytheism is belief in many gods and monotheism is belief in one.

check.q: Based on the stems, a hydrophobic surface does what?
check.why: Hydro means water and phobic means fearing or avoiding. A hydrophobic surface repels water.

lessons.title: Word Families Across Subjects
lessons.mainIdea: A single stem links words in science, math, history and art, so learning a word in one class helps you read another.
reading: Take the stem photo, from a Greek word meaning light. In art class, a photograph is a picture drawn by light. In biology, photosynthesis is how plants use light to put together, syn and thesis, their food. In physics, a photon is a particle of light. In technology, a photocopy is made by light bouncing off a page. One stem, four classes, one family of words.

Now take graph again. In English you write a paragraph. In math you plot a graph. In social studies you read about geography and demographics, which is writing about people, from demos, the Greek word for the people. Democracy, rule by the people, shares that stem. A student who learns demos in history can read demographics in a health class without stopping.

Families also cross into everyday life. The stem cycl means circle or wheel. A bicycle has two wheels. A cyclone is a circling storm. To recycle is to send something around again. An encyclopedia was named as a circle of learning. The water cycle in science goes around and around. Every new cycl word joins a family you already know.

Here is the payoff. Vocabulary in school is not thousands of separate words to memorize. It is a few hundred stems, prefixes and suffixes that recombine. Learn photo once and you get photograph, photosynthesis, photon, photocopy and telephoto. That is why this chapter teaches stems and not lists. A stem is a word you learn once and use in every class.

words.d: a Greek stem meaning light, as in photograph and photosynthesis
a Greek word meaning the people, the source of democracy and demographics
a Greek stem meaning circle or wheel, as in bicycle and recycle
the process by which plants use light to make their own food

look.title: One Family Tree
look.text: Photograph: a picture drawn by light. Photosynthesis: plants putting food together with light. Photon: a single particle of light. Photocopy: a copy made by light. Telephoto: a lens that brings far light close. Five words, five classrooms, one stem.
look.prompt: Pick a stem from earlier in the chapter and build your own family tree of at least four words. Which classes would you meet them in?

check.q: What does the stem photo mean in photosynthesis?
check.why: Photo means light. Photosynthesis is how plants use light to put together their food.

check.q: Which word belongs to the same family as democracy?
check.why: Both democracy and demographics are built on demos, the Greek word for the people.

check.q: Why does the lesson say vocabulary is not thousands of separate words?
choices: Because each class uses its own words
Because a few hundred parts recombine into many words
check.why: Stems, prefixes and suffixes recombine. Learning photo once gives you a whole family of words.

lessons.title: Unlocking a Test Word
lessons.mainIdea: When a strange word appears on a test or in a textbook, take it apart, build a meaning from the parts, then check it against the sentence.
reading: Marisol's method works in every class, and it has four steps. First, find a stem you know. Second, cut off any prefix at the front and any suffix at the end, and say what each one adds. Third, build a rough meaning from the pieces. Fourth, and this is the step people skip, check that meaning against the sentence. If it fits, keep going. If it does not, the word may have drifted from its roots, and you need another clue.

Try it on a social studies word: chronological. Chron, time. Logical, having to do with order or reason. Rough meaning: in time order. Check: the sentence says to put the events of the Revolution in chronological order. The meaning fits. Now try a science word: geothermal. Geo, earth. Thermal, from a Greek word for heat. Rough meaning: earth heat. Check: the passage describes power plants that use heat from deep underground. It fits.

Sometimes the check fails, and that matters. The word manufacture has manu, hand, and fact, make. The rough meaning is made by hand. But a sentence about a factory that manufactures cars with robots does not fit that meaning. The word has changed over centuries to mean made in a factory, by hand or not. The stems gave you a start; the sentence corrected it. Do both.

You can practice this in the Word Foundry and the class stem units on this site, which are practice rooms for taking words apart and putting them together. Do a few each week. The goal is not to know Greek. The goal is to sit down for a test, meet a word you never studied, and feel curious instead of stuck.

words.d: a first guess at a word's meaning, built from its parts before you check it in the sentence
having to do with heat from inside the earth; geo means earth and thermal means heat
to make something in a factory; the stems mean made by hand, though the meaning has changed

look.title: The Four Steps on a Test
look.text: A student meets the word antisocial on a health quiz. Step one: she spots the stem social, about being with people. Step two: she cuts off anti, against. Step three: rough meaning, against being with people. Step four: the sentence says antisocial behavior harms a community. The meaning fits, and she answers.
look.prompt: Try the four steps on the word dehydrated. What rough meaning do the parts give you, and what kind of sentence would confirm it?

check.q: What is the fourth step of the method, the one people often skip?
choices: Check the built meaning against the sentence
Look up the word in Greek
check.why: After building a rough meaning from the parts, you must check it against the sentence, because some words have drifted from their roots.

check.q: Why does the check fail for the word manufacture?
choices: The word's meaning has changed to include things made by machines
check.why: The stems mean made by hand, but the word now means made in a factory, so the sentence about robots corrects the rough meaning.

check.q: Using the method, what is a rough meaning for geothermal?
check.why: Geo means earth and thermal means heat. Geothermal energy comes from heat inside the earth.

review.q: Which part of a word carries its core meaning?
review.why: The stem carries the core meaning. Prefixes and suffixes change or adjust it.

review.q: Which group of stems is Greek and shows up mostly in science words?
review.why: Bio, geo and hydro are Greek stems, and Greek stems crowd into science and technology.

review.q: Based on its parts, what is a chronicle?
choices: A machine that makes sound louder
A record of events in time order
A story of the writer's own life
review.why: Chron means time. A chronicle records events in the order they happened.

review.q: Which word means to carry goods into a country?
review.why: Im means in and port means carry, so import means to carry goods in.

review.q: A story that cannot be believed is which of these?
review.why: In means not and cred means believe, so incredible means unbelievable.

review.q: What does the prefix anti mean in antibiotic?
review.why: Anti means against. An antibiotic works against the tiny living things that cause infection.

review.q: Which word belongs to the same family as photosynthesis?
review.why: Both are built on photo, the Greek stem meaning light.

review.q: Why should you check a built meaning against the sentence?
choices: Because Greek words have no meaning alone
Because some words have drifted away from what their parts mean
review.why: Manufacture is an example: its parts mean made by hand, but it now means made in a factory.

chapters.title: Connotation and Figurative Language
chapters.bigQuestion: How can two words with the same dictionary meaning, or a sentence that is not literally true, say completely different things?

story.title: The Classroom Was a Zoo
story.kicker: One sentence on the board, one word circled, and a class spends a period discovering how much a single word can carry.
paragraphs: Mr. Okafor wrote one sentence on the whiteboard before the bell rang: The classroom was a zoo. Then he circled the word zoo and sat down. The eighth graders filed in, read it and laughed, because it was true. The substitute the day before had lost control by second period. Somebody had taped a paper airplane to the ceiling. It was still there.

When the laughing stopped, he asked a simple question. Was the classroom actually a zoo? No, they said. No cages, no zebras. So the sentence was false. But everyone had understood it, and everyone had laughed. How? A girl in the back said that zoo did not mean zoo. It meant loud and wild and out of control, animals everywhere. The word had two layers: what it meant in the dictionary and what it made you feel.

Then Mr. Okafor gave the class a job. Replace zoo with any word that keeps the sentence true, and write the new sentence on the board. The markers came out. The classroom was a circus. The classroom was a stampede. The classroom was a storm. The classroom was a beehive. The classroom was a party. The classroom was a battlefield. Twelve sentences, twelve different rooms.

He read them aloud one at a time. A circus was chaos, but fun. A stampede was chaos and danger. A storm was chaos that nobody could stop. A beehive was busy, maybe even productive. A party was chaos that people enjoyed. A battlefield made the substitute sound like a wounded soldier. Every word had the same dictionary job, standing in for a loud, messy room. Every word gave a different feeling and told a different story.

That, he said, is the whole lesson. When you write, you choose words. Each word carries a feeling on its back, and some sentences work by saying something that is not literally true. A classroom is not a zoo. A heart does not break. Time does not fly. Yet these are some of the truest sentences in the language. This chapter is about how they work and how to write your own.
story.think: If you had to describe your loudest class with one word in the sentence The classroom was a ___, which word would you pick, and what feeling would it give a reader?

lessons.title: Denotation and Connotation
lessons.mainIdea: A word's denotation is its dictionary meaning, and its connotation is the feeling or association that rides along with it.
reading: Look at three words: thin, slender, scrawny. Open a dictionary and all three point at the same fact, a body without much fat on it. That shared dictionary meaning is the *denotation*. But nobody would be pleased to be called scrawny. Slender sounds graceful. Thin sounds neutral. Scrawny sounds weak and underfed. The feeling that comes with each word is its *connotation*.

Connotations can be positive, negative or neutral. A house is neutral. A home is warm. A shack is poor and falling apart. A mansion is rich. When a writer chooses one of these words, she is choosing a feeling for the reader, not just a building. Newspapers know this. A headline that says officials gathered feels calm. One that says officials huddled feels secretive.

Connotations come from how people have used a word over time. Cheap and inexpensive both mean low in price. But cheap has been used so often for badly made things that it now carries a sneer. Inexpensive stays polite. Stubborn and determined both mean unwilling to give up. One is a complaint, and the other is praise. Same behavior, different feelings.

Why does this matter to you? Because readers respond to connotation whether or not they notice it. If you write that a character stared, she seems intense. If you write that she gazed, she seems dreamy. If you write that she glared, she seems angry. You did not add a single adjective. You picked a verb with the right feeling on its back.

words.d: the plain dictionary meaning of a word
the feeling or association a word carries beyond its dictionary meaning
carrying no strong positive or negative feeling

look.title: Same Meaning, Different Feeling
rows: Words for a low price in the lesson
Words for a place to live in the lesson
Words for a way of looking in the lesson
Words for a thin body in the lesson
look.prompt: Pick one group and rank its words from most positive to most negative. Would everyone in your class rank them the same way?

check.q: Which word for a thin body has the most negative connotation?
check.why: Scrawny suggests weak and underfed. Slender sounds graceful and thin is close to neutral.

check.q: What is the denotation of a word?
choices: Its origin in Greek or Latin
check.why: Denotation is the literal dictionary meaning, shared by words like thin, slender and scrawny.

check.q: A writer replaces stared with glared. What changes?
check.why: Glared carries the connotation of anger. The verb's feeling changed while the basic action, looking, stayed the same.

lessons.title: Word Choice and Tone
lessons.mainIdea: Tone is the writer's attitude toward the subject, and it is built largely from the connotations of the words the writer chooses.
reading: Read two sentences about the same event. The crowd trickled into the old gym and settled onto the worn bleachers. The crowd crammed into the dingy gym and slumped onto the rickety bleachers. Same gym, same crowd, same night. The first sentence sounds fond and calm. The second sounds annoyed and a little disgusted. The difference is the writer's *tone*, the attitude that comes through the words.

Tone is not stated. It is built. Worn is gentle and even affectionate, the way a favorite jacket is worn. Dingy is dirty and depressing. Settled is peaceful. Slumped is tired and unhappy. Each word choice tips the sentence a little further toward one attitude. By the end, the reader knows exactly how the writer feels about that gym, though the writer never said so.

Writers control tone by choosing between words with the same denotation. A politician can be described as firm or as rigid. A meal can be simple or bland. A friend can be careful or timid. Readers, and especially test makers, will ask you to identify tone: admiring, mocking, sad, playful, angry, respectful. To answer, find the loaded words and ask what feeling they share.

Here is a quick test for your own writing. Underline the nouns, verbs and adjectives in a paragraph. Next to each, write plus, minus or zero for its connotation. If you wanted a warm paragraph and half your words are minus, you have found the problem. Tone is a total. Every word you pick either adds to it or fights it.

words.d: the writer's attitude toward the subject, shown through word choice and details
a word chosen for its strong positive or negative connotation
the way a person thinks or feels about something

look.title: Two Gyms
look.text: Version A: The crowd trickled into the old gym and settled onto the worn bleachers, and the band began. Version B: The crowd crammed into the dingy gym and slumped onto the rickety bleachers, and the band started up.
look.prompt: List the word pairs that differ between the two versions. For each pair, name the feeling each word carries and describe the tone of each version in one word.

check.q: What is tone?
choices: The dictionary meaning of a word
The writer's attitude toward the subject
The number of adjectives in a sentence
The sound a word makes when read aloud
check.why: Tone is the writer's attitude, which readers sense through word choices and details.

check.q: Which pair of words shows a positive and a negative connotation for the same behavior?
check.why: Firm is praise and rigid is a complaint, though both describe someone who does not bend.

check.q: How do readers usually figure out a writer's tone?
choices: By checking the date of publication
By finding the loaded words and asking what feeling they share
check.why: Tone is built from loaded words. Finding them and naming their shared feeling reveals the attitude.

lessons.title: A Thesaurus, Used Wisely
lessons.mainIdea: A thesaurus lists words with similar meanings, but its words are not interchangeable, so check the connotation and the sentence before you swap.
reading: A *thesaurus* is a book or a tool that lists synonyms, words with similar meanings. Type in walk and it offers stroll, march, trudge, saunter, stomp, wander and pace. That is useful when you have written walked six times in one paragraph. It is dangerous when you grab a word without knowing what it carries. A soldier marches. A tired hiker trudges. Nobody saunters into a burning building.

The classic mistake is trading a plain word for a fancy one to sound smart. A student writes, The dog was happy, checks the thesaurus, and produces, The canine was jubilant. Jubilant means wildly joyful, celebrating a victory. A dog wagging its tail is not jubilant. The fancy word is wrong, and it makes the sentence sound like a costume. Precise beats impressive.

Use the thesaurus in three steps. First, know what you mean exactly: not just walked, but walked slowly and sadly. Second, look at the list and pick a candidate that fits that exact meaning: trudged. Third, read the whole sentence with the new word out loud. If it sounds like something a real person would say, keep it. If it sounds like a costume, go back to the list or keep the plain word.

One more check: look up your new word in a dictionary, not just the thesaurus. The thesaurus tells you that words are neighbors. The dictionary tells you exactly how they differ. Together they let you choose the word with the right denotation and the right connotation for the sentence you are writing.

words.d: a reference tool that lists synonyms, words with similar meanings
a word with the same or nearly the same meaning as another word
exact; saying just what you mean and no more

look.title: Syllables in Synonyms for Walk
look.prompt: Longer words are not better words. Which of these would fit a tired hiker at the end of a long day, and which would fit a couple on a boardwalk?

check.q: What does a thesaurus list?
choices: Word origins from Greek and Latin
check.why: A thesaurus lists synonyms, words that mean the same or nearly the same as another word.

check.q: Why is The canine was jubilant a poor revision of The dog was happy?
choices: Jubilant means wildly joyful, which is too strong for a wagging dog
The sentence is now too short
check.why: Jubilant does not fit the exact meaning, so the fancy word makes the sentence sound false.

check.q: What is the last step before keeping a thesaurus word?
choices: Ask a friend if it sounds smart
Read the whole sentence aloud and check that it sounds real
Replace every other plain word too
check.why: Reading the sentence aloud tells you whether the new word fits or sounds like a costume.

lessons.title: Simile
lessons.mainIdea: A simile compares two unlike things using like or as, and the point of the comparison is to make one thing clearer or more vivid.
reading: Her voice was like gravel in a blender. You have never heard that voice, but you know it now: rough, loud, grinding. That sentence is a *simile*, a comparison between two unlike things using the word like or as. The voice is one thing. Gravel in a blender is another. Putting them side by side makes the voice instantly real.

Not every sentence with like is a simile. My brother is like my cousin compares two similar things, so it is just a plain comparison. A simile needs two things that do not belong together: a voice and gravel, a runner and a deer, a mind and a steel trap. The distance between them is where the surprise lives. The closer they are, the less the simile does.

A simile also needs a point. When you write as busy as a bee, ask what quality you are borrowing from the bee. Busyness. When Robert Burns wrote that his love was like a red, red rose that had newly sprung in June, he borrowed the rose's freshness and beauty. The comparison tells you which quality to notice. That is called the ground of the comparison.

Worn-out similes have lost their surprise: as cold as ice, as quiet as a mouse, as strong as an ox. They are so familiar that readers skip them. When you write your own, hunt for a comparison that is true and that nobody has used. The cafeteria line moved like a checkout on a holiday. The new teacher's handwriting looked like fallen fence posts. Fresh similes make readers see.

words.d: a comparison of two unlike things using like or as
words used in a way that is not literally true in order to create an effect
the shared quality that a comparison points to, such as the freshness a rose gives to a beloved

look.title: A Rose in June
look.text: O my Luve's like a red, red rose, / That's newly sprung in June: / O my Luve's like the melodie, / That's sweetly play'd in tune.
look.cite: Robert Burns, A Red, Red Rose, 1794
look.prompt: Burns uses two similes in four lines. What quality does each one borrow, the rose and the melody, and why might he have chosen June rather than another month?

check.q: Which sentence is a simile?
choices: The hallway was crowded and loud
My brother is like my cousin
The hallway roared like a subway platform at rush hour
The hallway was a subway platform
check.why: It compares two unlike things, a hallway and a subway platform, using like. Comparing similar things is not a simile, and the last choice has no like or as.

check.q: What does the ground of a comparison mean?
choices: The place where the comparison happens
The dictionary meaning of both words
The rhyme at the end of a line
The shared quality the comparison points to
check.why: The ground is the quality being borrowed, such as freshness from a rose or busyness from a bee.

check.q: Why do worn-out similes like as cold as ice weaken writing?
choices: Readers skip them because they are too familiar
They use as instead of like
check.why: Overused similes have lost their surprise, so readers no longer picture anything.

lessons.title: Metaphor
lessons.mainIdea: A metaphor says one thing is another, without like or as, so the reader carries the qualities of one over onto the other.
reading: The classroom was a zoo. No like, no as. The sentence does not say the room was like a zoo; it says the room was a zoo. That is a *metaphor*, a comparison that states one thing is another. Because it drops the like, a metaphor is bolder than a simile. It asks the reader to hold two pictures in one place: a classroom and a zoo, a heart and a stone, a city and a jungle.

Metaphors can hide in verbs and adjectives too, not just in is sentences. Prices soared. A voice cut through the noise. She drowned in homework. Nobody flew, nothing was sliced, no one got wet. Each verb quietly compares one thing to another. Prices are treated like a bird, a voice like a knife, homework like water. Once you notice these hidden metaphors, you find them everywhere, even in science and math class.

Shakespeare's Jaques begins a famous speech with a metaphor: All the world's a stage, and all the men and women merely players. The world is not a stage. But once you accept the comparison, the rest follows. People enter, play their parts and exit. An extended metaphor like this one keeps building on the same comparison for a whole passage.

When you read a metaphor, ask two questions. What two things are being compared? And what quality moves from one to the other? In Time is money, time is compared to money, and the quality that moves is value: time can be spent, saved or wasted. Answer those two questions and you have interpreted the metaphor.

words.d: a comparison that says one thing is another, without like or as
a metaphor that continues and develops through several sentences or lines
meaning exactly what the words say, with no comparison or exaggeration

look.title: The World as a Stage
look.text: All the world's a stage, / And all the men and women merely players; / They have their exits and their entrances; / And one man in his time plays many parts.
look.cite: William Shakespeare, As You Like It, Act 2, Scene 7, about 1599
look.prompt: What two things does this metaphor compare? List three details from the stage that Shakespeare carries over to human life in these four lines.

check.q: How does a metaphor differ from a simile?
choices: A metaphor uses like or as
A metaphor states that one thing is another, without like or as
A metaphor compares two similar things
A metaphor is always about animals
check.why: A simile uses like or as. A metaphor drops those words and says the thing simply is the other thing.

check.q: In the sentence Prices soared, what hidden comparison is at work?
choices: Prices are compared to a knife
Prices are compared to a bird or something that flies
check.why: Soared is a verb for flight. The sentence treats prices as if they flew upward.

check.q: What is an extended metaphor?
choices: A metaphor that is longer than ten words
A metaphor in a poem only
A metaphor that uses both like and as
A metaphor that keeps developing over a whole passage
check.why: Shakespeare's stage metaphor continues for many lines, adding entrances, exits and parts.

lessons.title: Personification
lessons.mainIdea: Personification gives human actions, feelings or qualities to something that is not human, so the reader relates to it as if it were alive.
reading: The wind moaned around the corner of the house. The old truck coughed, groaned and finally refused to start. Wind cannot moan and a truck cannot refuse. Those sentences use *personification*, giving human actions or feelings to something that is not a person. The technique is old and everywhere: the sun smiles, the flowers dance, the alarm clock screams, the city never sleeps.

Personification works because people understand people. If a writer says the fog came in on little cat feet, as Carl Sandburg did in his 1916 poem about Chicago fog, you feel how quietly it arrives and how it seems to sit and watch before it moves on. Sandburg gives the fog a cat's body. Emily Dickinson goes further in a poem that begins, Because I could not stop for Death, He kindly stopped for me. Death becomes a polite driver with a carriage.

Personification is a kind of metaphor. It compares a thing to a person and carries over one human quality: patience, anger, kindness, stubbornness. A good one picks the quality carefully. The refrigerator hummed a lazy tune tells you the kitchen is calm. The refrigerator growled tells you something is wrong with it, or with the mood in the room.

When you write, use personification to give a mood to a place or a thing. Do not pile it up. One moaning wind sets a scene. Five moaning, sobbing, shrieking, whispering, sighing winds in one paragraph turn a scene into a joke. Choose one human action, make it exact, and move on.

words.d: giving human actions, feelings or qualities to something that is not human
the feeling a piece of writing creates in the reader
a feature or characteristic of a person or thing, such as patience or anger

look.title: Fog on Cat Feet
look.text: The fog comes / on little cat feet. / It sits looking / over harbor and city / on silent haunches / and then moves on.
look.cite: Carl Sandburg, Fog, from Chicago Poems, 1916
look.prompt: Which words give the fog a cat's body? What do you learn about how the fog moves and how long it stays that you would not learn from The fog rolled in?

check.q: Which sentence uses personification?
choices: The wind moaned around the corner of the house
The wind was as cold as ice
The wind blew at forty miles per hour
check.why: Moaning is a human action given to the wind. The second is a simile, the third is literal and the fourth is a metaphor that does not make the wind human.

check.q: In Sandburg's poem, what does the fog borrow from a cat?
choices: Its quiet arrival and its way of sitting and watching
check.why: The fog comes on little cat feet and sits on silent haunches, so it borrows a cat's silence and stillness.

check.q: Why does the lesson warn against piling up personification?
choices: It is only allowed in poems
Too many human actions in one paragraph turn a scene into a joke
It makes the sentence a simile
check.why: One exact human action sets a mood. Five in a row become silly and lose their effect.

lessons.title: Hyperbole
lessons.mainIdea: Hyperbole is deliberate exaggeration for effect; the reader is not supposed to believe it literally but to feel the size of the feeling.
reading: I have told you a million times. My backpack weighs a ton. I could eat a horse. Nobody has said anything a million times, backpacks weigh a few pounds and no one eats a horse. These are *hyperbole*, exaggeration on purpose. The speaker does not expect to be believed. The exaggeration measures a feeling: frustration, weariness, hunger. The bigger the stretch, the bigger the feeling.

Hyperbole is a favorite of tall tales. American folklore has Paul Bunyan, a lumberjack so huge his footprints filled with water and became lakes, and Pecos Bill, who rode a tornado. Nobody believes it, and that is the fun. Comedians use hyperbole constantly. So do sports announcers: the fastest player who ever lived, a catch nobody else on Earth could make.

The danger with hyperbole is that it can hide behind a fact. An ad that says everybody is switching to this phone is hyperbole dressed as news. A friend who says you never listen is exaggerating in the middle of a real argument. When you read, ask whether a big claim is measured or stretched. When you write an argument essay, avoid it; readers who catch one stretch stop trusting your numbers.

In stories and poems, though, hyperbole is a tool. It shows how a character feels from the inside. A boy who says the walk to the principal's office took a hundred years is telling you about dread, not distance. The exaggeration is the truth about the feeling, delivered by a lie about the fact.

words.d: deliberate exaggeration used for effect, not meant to be taken literally
a story with wildly exaggerated events and a larger-than-life hero, such as Paul Bunyan
the opposite of hyperbole: describing something as smaller or less important than it is

look.title: A Hundred Years to the Office
look.text: A sixth grader is sent to the principal's office. Later he writes: The hallway stretched for ten miles. Every locker stared at me. The walk took a hundred years and my heart was a drum somebody was beating with a hammer. Not one sentence is literally true. Every sentence is exactly how it felt.
look.prompt: Find the hyperbole, the personification and the metaphor in the student's four sentences. Which one tells you most about how he felt?

check.q: What is hyperbole?
choices: A comparison using like or as
Giving human qualities to a thing
check.why: Hyperbole stretches the truth on purpose so the reader feels the size of a feeling.

check.q: Why does the lesson say to avoid hyperbole in an argument essay?
choices: It is too hard to spell
Readers who catch a stretch stop trusting the writer's other claims
It makes the essay too short
check.why: In an argument, one exaggeration makes readers doubt the rest of your evidence.

check.q: A boy says the walk to the office took a hundred years. What is the sentence really about?
check.why: The exaggeration measures a feeling, dread, not the actual time.

lessons.title: Allusion
lessons.mainIdea: An allusion is a brief reference to a well-known story, person, place or event that the reader is expected to recognize.
reading: A coach says the new quarterback is the team's Achilles' heel. A reporter calls a proposal a Trojan horse. A teacher warns that a plan will open Pandora's box. None of these people are talking about ancient Greece. They are using an *allusion*, a quick reference to a story the listener is expected to know, so that the whole story's meaning arrives in two or three words.

Each of those allusions carries a story. Achilles was a Greek hero who could not be wounded anywhere except his heel, so an Achilles' heel is a single weak spot. The Trojan horse was a gift that hid enemy soldiers, so a Trojan horse is something harmful disguised as something good. Pandora opened a box and released troubles into the world, so opening Pandora's box means starting problems you cannot stop.

Allusions come from everywhere people share stories: myths, the Bible, history, fairy tales, famous books, movies and songs. Calling someone a Scrooge alludes to Dickens. Saying a place is no Garden of Eden alludes to the Bible. Calling a bad decision a Titanic alludes to the 1912 shipwreck. If you do not know the story, the allusion goes past you. That is a reason to read widely.

When you meet a name or phrase that seems to come from nowhere, treat it as a possible allusion. Ask: is this a story I half know? Look it up. Then ask what quality the writer is borrowing. An allusion works exactly like a metaphor, except that the second half of the comparison is a story you have to supply yourself.

words.d: a brief reference to a well-known story, person, place or event
a single weak spot in someone or something otherwise strong, from the Greek hero Achilles
something harmful disguised as a gift, from the Greek story of the wooden horse that hid soldiers

look.title: Three Allusions at Lunch
look.text: At a lunch table, one student says the math test was her Waterloo, another says the sub was a real Scrooge, and a third says trying to find the lost hall pass was a wild goose chase. The first alludes to the 1815 battle Napoleon lost, the second to a Dickens character and the third to an old expression for a hopeless search.
look.prompt: Which of the three allusions would most students at your school recognize? What happens to the sentence if the listener does not know the story?

check.q: What is an allusion?
choices: A brief reference to a well-known story, person or event
A word with a negative feeling
check.why: An allusion points to a story the reader already knows so its meaning arrives quickly.

check.q: Based on the lesson, what does it mean to call a plan a Trojan horse?
choices: It hides something harmful inside something that looks good
check.why: The Trojan horse was a gift that hid enemy soldiers, so the allusion means a disguised danger.

check.q: What happens if a reader does not know the story behind an allusion?
choices: The reader misses the meaning the writer intended
check.why: An allusion depends on shared knowledge. Without the story, the reference goes past the reader.

lessons.title: Idiom
lessons.mainIdea: An idiom is a fixed expression whose meaning cannot be figured out from its individual words, so it must be learned as a whole.
reading: It is raining cats and dogs. He let the cat out of the bag. She hit the books. These are *idioms*, phrases whose meaning is not the sum of their words. No animals fall from the sky. Hitting a book does not help you study. An idiom has to be learned whole, the way you learn a single word. Every language has thousands, and they are one of the hardest parts of learning a new language.

Idioms are a special problem for readers who are learning English, and an unfair one, because the words are all easy. Break a leg means good luck. Piece of cake means easy. Under the weather means sick. Cost an arm and a leg means expensive. If you take these literally, the sentence turns strange. If you know them, they are as clear as any word. When a sentence with simple words makes no sense, suspect an idiom and look it up.

Idioms differ from metaphors in one way. A fresh metaphor is invented by a writer and asks you to picture two things. An idiom was a metaphor once, maybe centuries ago, but the picture has faded. When someone says she spilled the beans, nobody sees beans. The phrase now just means told the secret. Idioms are metaphors that have gone to sleep.

In your own writing, idioms make dialogue sound natural, because real people use them all the time. In formal writing, they can sound sloppy, and a reader from another country may not understand them. A science report should say the results were unexpected, not the results came out of left field. Know which room you are writing in.

words.d: a fixed expression whose meaning cannot be figured out from its individual words
in the exact, word-for-word sense, with no figure of speech
writing for school, work or the public that follows standard rules and avoids slang

look.title: Idioms in a Model Paragraph
look.cite: counted for this lesson from the idioms listed in the reading
look.prompt: Why might so many idioms use animals, bodies, food and weather? What do those four things have in common for the people who first made up the phrases?

check.q: Which statement about idioms is true?
choices: Their meaning is the sum of their words
They must be learned as whole expressions
They are used only in poems
check.why: An idiom's meaning cannot be built from its parts, so it is learned whole, like a single word.

check.q: Why are idioms especially hard for someone learning English?
choices: The words are difficult to spell
The words are easy, but the meaning of the phrase is not what the words say
check.why: Idioms use simple words, so the reader assumes the literal meaning and the sentence turns strange.

check.q: How does an idiom differ from a fresh metaphor?
choices: An idiom uses like or as
An idiom is only found in poetry
An idiom's picture has faded, while a fresh metaphor makes the reader picture two things
check.why: Idioms are old metaphors whose images have worn away. Spilled the beans no longer makes anyone see beans.

lessons.title: Analogies
lessons.mainIdea: An analogy explains something unfamiliar by comparing it to something familiar, and on tests it appears as a pair of word pairs with the same relationship.
reading: A teacher explaining the heart says it is like a pump in a house's plumbing: a muscle that pushes fluid through pipes to every room. That is an *analogy*, a comparison that explains how something unfamiliar works by matching it to something you already understand. Analogies are longer and more practical than similes. Their job is not surprise but understanding.

On tests, analogies often appear in a compressed form: puppy is to dog as kitten is to cat. The two pairs share a relationship. A puppy is a young dog; a kitten is a young cat. To solve one, find the relationship in the first pair and state it in a sentence. Then check that the same sentence works for the second pair. Hot is to cold as up is to down: both pairs are opposites.

Common relationships include part to whole, such as petal is to flower; worker to tool, such as carpenter is to hammer; cause to effect, such as rain is to flood; word to synonym or antonym; and category to member, such as fruit is to apple. Write the relationship as a sentence and the puzzle usually opens. If two answer choices both seem to fit, make your sentence more exact.

Analogies also drive good explanations in science and history. An atom is like a tiny solar system. A cell membrane is like a security guard at a door. The colonies under Britain were like teenagers with a strict parent. Each analogy is imperfect, and part of thinking well is knowing where it breaks down. Electrons do not orbit like planets. But as a first step, a good analogy carries a reader most of the way.

words.d: a comparison that explains something unfamiliar by matching it to something familiar
the connection between two things, such as part to whole or cause to effect
a group that things belong to; fruit is the category and apple is a member

look.title: Solving One on a Test
look.text: The test says: Petal is to flower as ___ is to tree. The choices are leaf, forest, bark and oak. A student writes the relationship as a sentence: a petal is a part of a flower. Then she tries each choice. A forest is not part of a tree. An oak is a kind of tree, not a part. Bark and leaf are both parts. She makes her sentence more exact: a petal is a part that grows off a flower and can fall off.
look.prompt: Which answer does the more exact sentence point to? Write your own analogy in the same form using the relationship worker to tool.

check.q: What is the main job of an analogy?
choices: To help someone understand something unfamiliar
To give a thing human qualities
check.why: An analogy explains by matching the unknown to the known, like the heart to a pump.

check.q: What is the first step in solving puppy is to dog as kitten is to ___?
choices: State the relationship of the first pair in a sentence
Look up puppy in a thesaurus
Count the letters in each word
check.why: Find the relationship, a puppy is a young dog, then test the same sentence on the second pair.

check.q: Rain is to flood shows which kind of relationship?
check.why: Rain causes a flood, so the pair shows cause to effect.

lessons.title: Figures in Poems and Ads
lessons.mainIdea: Poets and advertisers both use figurative language, and interpreting a figure means finding the comparison and asking what feeling or idea it delivers.
reading: A poem uses figures of speech to make a reader feel something exact in a small space. Emily Dickinson begins a poem, Hope is the thing with feathers, that perches in the soul. Hope has no feathers. But once hope is a bird, the poem can say it sings without words and never stops. To interpret the figure, ask: what is compared to what, and why that thing? A bird is small, alive, light and hard to catch. So is hope.

Ads use the same tools for a different reason: to make you want something. A car ad says the new model is a beast. A phone is your window to the world. A cereal gives you a mountain of energy. Beast is a metaphor for power. Window is a metaphor for access. Mountain is hyperbole. The ad borrows a feeling from the image and pins it on the product. The poem wants you to see. The ad wants you to buy.

Both depend on context. The word beast in a car ad means powerful. The word beast in a story about a barn means a farm animal. The same word in a sentence about a rude person means cruel. You cannot interpret a figure by itself; you read the sentences around it and ask which meaning fits. Test questions on figurative language almost always give you a passage for this reason.

Here is a habit for both poems and ads. When a sentence cannot be literally true, stop. Name the figure: simile, metaphor, personification, hyperbole, allusion or idiom. Say what two things are compared. Say what quality moves across. Then ask what the writer wants from you. A poet wants you to see and feel. An advertiser wants your money. Knowing the difference is part of reading.

words.d: a word or phrase used in a way that is not literally true, such as a metaphor or simile
to explain what something means
the words and sentences around a word that help show which meaning is intended

look.title: Hope with Feathers
look.text: “Hope” is the thing with feathers - / That perches in the soul - / And sings the tune without the words - / And never stops - at all -
look.cite: Emily Dickinson, poem written about 1861, published 1891
look.prompt: Dickinson never uses the word bird. Which words tell you that hope is a bird? What does each borrowed bird quality say about hope?

check.q: In Dickinson's poem, what is hope compared to?
check.why: Hope has feathers, perches and sings, all actions and features of a bird, though the poem never uses the word.

check.q: A car ad calls the new model a beast. What does the metaphor deliver?
choices: That the car is an animal
That the car is dangerous to drive
check.why: In the context of a car ad, beast borrows the quality of raw power.

check.q: Why do test questions about figurative language usually give a whole passage?
choices: Because a figure's meaning depends on the context around it
Because passages are easier to print
Because figures of speech only appear in long texts
check.why: The same word, like beast, means different things in different contexts, so you need the surrounding sentences to interpret it.

lessons.title: Precise Language in Your Writing
lessons.mainIdea: Strong writing uses exact words and fresh figures where they help, and cuts vague words, worn-out figures and exaggeration that readers will not believe.
reading: Read this sentence: The weather was bad and the game was really fun anyway. Now read this one: Sleet needled our faces, and we played the whole second half laughing. The first is vague. Bad and fun and really tell the reader almost nothing. The second is *precise*. Sleet is exact. Needled is a metaphor that makes the sting real. Laughing shows the fun instead of announcing it.

Precision starts with nouns and verbs. Do not write a bird flew when you mean a hawk circled. Do not write she went when you mean she stomped, drifted or sprinted. Replace very tired with exhausted, very big with enormous, very small with tiny. A specific noun or verb usually does more than a plain one plus an adverb. Then check your connotations. Does each word carry the feeling you want?

Add figures of speech the way a cook adds salt: where they sharpen the taste, and not everywhere. One fresh simile in a paragraph makes a reader see. Three make the reader tired. Cut clichés, the worn-out figures like as cold as ice and busy as a bee. Cut hyperbole from anything that needs to be believed. Keep an idiom in dialogue if a real person would say it, and cut it from a formal report.

Revise with a list of questions. Is each noun the most specific one? Is each verb doing real work? Does every connotation match my tone? Is every figure fresh, and does it carry the right quality? Would a reader who does not know me understand every idiom? If the answer is yes all the way down, your sentence is doing what you meant it to do. That is what precise language means.

words.d: exact; naming just what you mean
unclear or general; not specific
a phrase or figure of speech that has been used so often it has lost its effect

look.title: Two Versions of One Sentence
look.text: Version A: The weather was bad and the game was really fun anyway. Version B: Sleet needled our faces, and we played the whole second half laughing.
look.prompt: List the changes from A to B. Which changes replace a vague word with an exact one, and which add a figure of speech? Rewrite a vague sentence of your own the same way.

check.q: Which revision replaces a vague phrase with a precise one?
choices: very tired becomes really very tired
check.why: Exhausted is a specific word that does more than a plain word plus an adverb.

check.q: What is a cliché?
choices: A word with a negative connotation
A comparison using like or as
A figure of speech worn out by overuse
A word from Greek or Latin
check.why: Phrases like as cold as ice have been used so often that readers no longer picture anything.

check.q: Why does the lesson compare figures of speech to salt?
choices: Because they only belong in cooking writing
Because a little sharpens the writing and too much spoils it
check.why: One fresh figure helps a reader see; several in a row make the reader tired.

review.q: Which word has the most positive connotation?
review.why: Home carries warmth. House and dwelling are neutral, and shack is negative.

review.q: A writer describes a gym with the words dingy, rickety and slumped. What is the tone?
review.why: All three words carry negative connotations, so together they build an unhappy, critical tone.

choices: The moon was a silver coin
The moon watched over the town
The moon hung like a lantern over the town
The moon rose at nine o'clock
review.why: It compares the moon to a lantern using like. The first is a metaphor, the second personification and the fourth literal.

choices: The engine was as loud as thunder
The engine ran for six hours
The engine grumbled and refused to start
review.why: Grumbling and refusing are human actions given to a machine.

review.q: My backpack weighs a ton is an example of what?
review.why: It is a deliberate exaggeration meant to show how heavy the backpack feels, not a fact.

review.q: Calling a weak spot an Achilles' heel is an example of what?
choices: An idiom that cannot be looked up
An allusion to a well-known story
review.why: It refers to the Greek hero Achilles, whose only weak spot was his heel, so it is an allusion.

review.q: Why can idioms be hard for someone learning English?
choices: The words are rare and long
They appear only in old poems
The words are simple but the meaning is not what the words say
review.why: Piece of cake uses easy words, but a literal reading makes no sense. The phrase must be learned whole.

review.q: Which is the best advice for using a thesaurus?
choices: Pick the longest synonym to sound smart
Replace every plain word in the paragraph
Choose the synonym with the exact meaning and read the sentence aloud to check it
review.why: Synonyms are not interchangeable. Check the exact meaning and connotation before swapping.
